definition: The first day of the month in the Roman calendar; by extension, any reckoning point or starting date of a cycle.
etymology: From Latin Kalendae, the name Romans gave to the first day of each month, itself from calare, meaning to announce or to proclaim — because on that day a priest would call out how many days remained until the Nones. The word gave us calendar, that most ordinary of objects, still carrying inside it the echo of a herald's voice.
usage: July arrives on its calends with the particular confidence of a month that knows it owns the summer.
